t: #3409 Longest Subsequence With Decreasing Adjacent Difference
o: We need the longest subsequence whose consecutive absolute differences are non-increasing. Values are bounded by 300, so differences live in [0, 300] — a perfect DP dimension. Define g[v][d] = length of the longest valid subsequence ending at value v whose last adjacent difference is at least d (suffix-max encoding). When appending x after y with d = |x−y|, the new length is g[y][d] + 1; then fold results into g[x][·] with a suffix maximum.
k: Bounding values by 300 bounds differences by 300, enabling a value×difference DP table of only ~90k entries.
Storing 'last difference ≥ d' (suffix maxima) lets each transition be an O(1) lookup instead of scanning all smaller differences.
Per element we only iterate over previously SEEN values (≤ 300 distinct), giving O(n · 300) total.

a.n: Approach 1: Value × Difference DP with Suffix Maxima
a.i: g[v][d] = best length ending at value v with last difference ≥ d; g[v][301] = 1 covers length-1 subsequences. For each new x, query g[y][|x−y|] for every seen y, collect per-difference bests, convert to suffix maxima, and merge into row g[x].
s: Initialize g[v][301] = 1 for all v; keep a set of seen values.
For each x: for each seen y, d = |x−y|, tmp[d] = max(tmp[d], g[y][d] + 1); also tmp[301] = 1.
Suffix-max tmp over d descending, then element-wise max-merge into g[x].
Track the global maximum; return it.
a.t: O(n · V) with V = 300 distinct values — each element scans seen values and a 302-length suffix pass; ~3×10^6 core operations.
a.sp: O(V · D) = O(301 × 303) — the DP table, independent of n.

w: This DP is the intended solution; the naive O(n²) pairwise DP with per-pair suffix queries degrades badly in Python. Make sure to explain the '≥ d' suffix-max trick — it collapses the inner dimension of the transition. Pitfalls: forgetting the length-1 base (tmp[MAXD] = 1), iterating d downward for the suffix max, and answering with tmp[1] (constraint-free best ending at x). Edge cases: strictly increasing or constant arrays (answer 2 for constant? — [5,5] has difference 0,0 non-increasing, so longer runs of equal values count). Follow-up: reconstruct the subsequence, or handle values up to 10^9 (coordinate compression won't preserve difference structure — a genuinely harder variant).
